extraction.name: SeamlessM4T: Massively Multilingual & Multimodal Machine Translation
extraction.description: A unified multilingual and multimodal machine translation system supporting ASR, S2TT, T2ST, T2TT, and S2ST for up to 100 languages, built using open speech audio, automatically aligned speech translations, human-labeled data, and pseudo-labeled data.
extraction.creator: Meta AI Research / Seamless Communication et al.
extraction.citeAs: Seamless Communication et al., SeamlessM4T: Massively Multilingual & Multimodal Machine Translation, arXiv, 2023.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The paper describes a data collection and mining workflow that starts from a large collection of raw audio from a publicly available repository of crawled web data and uses speech language identification, voice activity detection, over-segmentation, and embedding-based mining to create SeamlessAlign. On the text side, it relies on the same sentence-segmented dataset used in NLLB. The assembled training data also includes human-labeled and pseudo-labeled data.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator, Experiments
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Some samples from the CVSS evaluation data were missing in 8 out of 21 languages: Catalan, German, Estonian, French, Italian, Mongolian, Persian, and Portuguese.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: 4 million hours of raw audio originating from a publicly available repository of crawled web data; sentence-segmented text data drawn from NLLB; human-labeled ASR transcriptions; pseudo-labeled ASR data; mined speech-text and speech-speech alignments from SeamlessAlign.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Raw audio URLs were deduplicated, audio files were downloaded and resampled at 16 kHz, non-speech data was filtered with an audio event detection model, audio was segmented with Voice Activity Detection and over-segmentation, and mined pairs were filtered using thresholds on LID scores, toxicity imbalance, utterance duration, text length, emoji/punctuation/space ratios, and alignment scores.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Text data used the same cleaning and filtering steps as NLLB and was processed at scale with Stopes. Human-labeled S2TT data had special tokens such as <silence> and <no-speech> removed, and examples were filtered by maximum text length and text-to-audio length ratio. Additional filtering removed utterances shorter than 0.1 seconds or longer than 50 seconds, texts longer than 250 sub-words, and texts with excessive emojis, punctuation, or spaces.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human evaluation annotations were created using the XSTS protocol for translation quality and MOS for speech naturalness/clarity/sound quality. For XSTS, 3 annotators evaluated each item; if their scores differed by 2 or more, 2 additional annotators were added. The median score was used. For MOS, annotators provided Likert scores from 1 to 5.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: XSTS scores were calibrated using a cross-lingual calibration set and moderated calibration methodology. The median over annotators was used for robustness, and language-level scores were calibrated using the mean score on the calibration set. For MOS, the median of annotator scores was used and no calibration was performed.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: XSTS: 3 annotators per item, with up to 5 when there was a disagreement of 2 or more score values; MOS: typically 3 annotators per item, but some languages had only 1 annotator per item.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Not explicitly specified; annotators were described as team members for the human error analysis of toxicity, and vendor annotators were used for evaluation work. The paper notes that when preparing Fleurs for human reference evaluation, pairings were made to match user gender when possible.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Whisper-Large-v2 and Whisper-Medium were used for ASR-based evaluation and toxicity detection pipelines; ETOX was used for toxicity detection; Sonar embeddings and Blaser 2.0 were used for model-based evaluation; FAISS and Stopes were used in mining and processing pipelines.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The paper states that models, inference code, finetuning recipes, and metadata to recreate the unfiltered 470,000 hours of SeamlessAlign are open-sourced at the project repository. It also notes that the optimal mining threshold can be tuned based on task needs and that future iterations may expand mining to all 100 languages. No formal versioning or deprecation policy is provided.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The paper discusses and evaluates gender, language, geography, age, culture, socio-economic class, race/ethnicity, religion, nationality, sexual orientation, ability, and speaker variation as sensitive or demographic attributes. It also notes that personally identifiable information may not be entirely eliminated from web-mined training data.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper argues that the system could improve accessibility, multilingual communication, and world-readiness, especially for low-resource language communities and people with visual impairments or limited literacy. It also warns that the technology could be misused for misinformation or scams and that toxic, biased, or false outputs could adversely affect users in high-stakes settings.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper reports gender bias, including overgeneralization toward masculine forms when translating from neutral inputs, and differences in performance between masculine and feminine forms. It also notes overrepresentation of masculine lexica in analyzed datasets and language-dependent variation in toxicity distributions.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The model is trained on short text and speech inputs and is not intended for long-form translation, domain-specific inputs, or certified translations. Human evaluation is limited by the Fleurs test set, limited speaker diversity, and small annotator samples. Toxicity and gender-bias detection rely on string matching and have known limitations, especially for non-segmenting or agglutinative languages and for speech outputs where ASR introduces errors.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Primary intended uses are research in speech and text translation, including ASR, S2ST, S2TT, T2ST, T2TT, and TTS. The model is intended for training, evaluation, and fine-tuning research workflows, not production deployment.
